title: In Jericho, Israeli Settlers Violently Seize and Occupy Palestinian Homes
author: Katrine Dige Houmøller

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F90d3929e-95c3-47df-8c7b-6fb8c035b97e_6240x4160.jpeg)An
Israeli soldier places his hand on the shoulder of an armed Israeli settler in
the Al-Duyuk Al-Tahta neighborhood of Jericho, in the occupied West Bank, on
November 5, 2026, a day after settlers violently seized Palestinian homes in
the neighborhood. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller for Drop Site News.

JERICHO, Occupied West Bank--"They beat all of us. Children, women, and men,"
Mustafa Kaaba said, standing on a dusty street in the city of Jericho in the
occupied West Bank. The night before, November 4, armed Israeli settlers burst
into his home and the homes of his neighbors, ransacking them, violently
forcing the families out, and warning them not to return.

Kaaba clutched his head and struggled to lift his arm, which was visibly
swollen and bruised after settlers beat him with sticks. Around him, his
family's belongings lay scattered across the street. Kaaba's pregnant wife,
Fatima, gathered what was left of their clothes and stuffed them into plastic
bags. After being expelled from their home, the family of seven was forced to
sleep in their car and on the street.

"They ripped up the children's schoolbooks and books written in Arabic,"
Fatima told Drop Site. "They didn't even leave our children anything to study
with." Fatima said the settlers took their refrigerator, washing machine,
television, and entire bedroom set to another apartment seized by the
settlers.

Around her, children ran between piles of rubble and scattered sheep that
wandered out from a nearby corrugated metal shed. The couple's young daughter
had been in a playful mood, running up to people for hugs. Then, without
warning, she burst into tears, screaming and running away from those around
her. Her father tried in vain to comfort her. "She is having a panic attack,"
Kaaba said. "I think it's triggered by the trauma from last night."

The family is now afraid to walk around Al-Duyuk Al-Tahta, their neighborhood
on the outskirts of the city. "It's dangerous, even just getting to the end of
this street. I swear, it's dangerous. What if they come after us?" Kaaba said.
"We don't have anything left."

Fatima stood nearby clutching a piece of clothing. "Our house is still
standing, but they told us not to come back," she added. "They say it belongs
to them now."

According to residents, at least 13 Palestinian households were driven from
their homes in Jericho by some 30 Israeli settlers, some of them masked, who
rampaged through the neighborhood.

The next morning, the settlers made their occupation known. They hung Israeli
flags from the balconies and entrances of multiple houses--a standard marker
of a Palestinian home taken over by settlers. Armed men patrolled between the
newly occupied homes--with rifles slung over their shoulders or pistols tucked
into their waistbands. Israeli women and children wandered along the gravel
roads. Young men sat outside reading the Torah while gunmen stood guard at
every property.

The expansion of Israeli settlements and outposts across the occupied West
Bank over the past three years has been rapid and increasingly violent. More
than 6,400 Palestinians, including over 3,100 children, were displaced between
January 2023 and August 2026 as a result of settler attacks and restrictions
on access to their land,
[according](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/occupied-palestinian-
territory/opt-humanitarian-situation-report-4-september-2026) to the UN Office
for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. At least 48 Palestinian
communities were completely emptied of their residents during that period.

Even in that context, the takeover by Israeli settlers of homes inside a
Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank represents a dangerous escalation
in Israel's dispossession of Palestinians across the territory. Some
Palestinians are comparing it to the situation in Hebron, the largest city in
the West Bank and the only one to have Israeli settlements inside the heart of
the city.

Most Israeli settlements surround Palestinian towns and cities, usually on the
surrounding hilltops, but in Hebron armed Israeli settlers live in the midst
of Palestinian residents and are guarded by a permanent and large deployment
of Israeli troops, making Hebron one of the most [tightly
controlled](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/hebron-forced-displacement-israeli-
operation) and ethnically segregated urban areas in the West Bank with
Palestinians even prevented from walking down certain streets.

"Establishing a settlement inside Jericho poses a security threat and
constitutes a geopolitical disaster that must not be allowed to happen. This
move is designed to deepen friction and violence, entrench an apartheid
regime, and foreclose any possibility of a future political agreement," the
Israeli group Peace Now, that organizes against settlements in the West Bank,
warned in a [statement](https://peacenow.org.il/en/settlers-establish-a-new-
settlement-in-the-city-of-jericho).

The violent home seizures on Wednesday came after a gradual buildup. The
neighborhood of Al-Duyuk Al-Tahta had been experiencing repeated attacks by
settlers, often from a nearby outpost called Palace Farms, according to Peace
Now. Settlers also demolished around 13 homes in the area in February and
again in July. Rubble is still scattered throughout the neighborhood.

By October 27, the day of the Israeli elections, settlers had already begun
fencing off parts of the neighborhood and installing infrastructure, according
to Peace Now, which also reported a number of break-ins, thefts, and assaults
on residents. A gate was erected to block access to an entire street, cutting
off dozens of Palestinian homes. Now, the settlers have taken over some of
those homes.

The Israeli military did nothing to stop the violent takeover, with multiple
Palestinian residents telling Drop Site that troops stood by as families were
forced out.

The following morning, Israeli military vehicles repeatedly drove through the
neighborhood. Uniformed soldiers warmly greeted the settlers, shook hands, and
embraced them. Some entered the occupied houses, appearing familiar with the
settlers inside.

Outside one of the newly occupied properties, a settler sat in a chair keeping
guard. "They're good friends of the families now," he said as soldiers walked
into the house. "Since last night," he added.

The properties are located on the outskirts of Jericho and technically in Area
C--a designation under the Oslo Accords of the 1990s where Israel retains full
civil and military control--right on the border of Area A, where the
Palestinian Authority has nominal security and civil control, and where most
of Jericho city is located.

The takeover was reportedly coordinated by the settlement organization Nachala
and the Binyamin Regional Council. Both organizations claim that the
properties were legally purchased. Jericho Governor Hussein Hamayel disputed
the claims, saying in an interview with Raya Media Network that the land
belongs to Jordan's state treasury and describing the alleged sales as forged.

In response to an inquiry from Drop Site, about the Israeli military's role in
the takeover, accounts of violence and looting by settlers, and the settlers'
continued occupation of the Palestinian homes, a military official said in a
written response that "Upon the entry of Israeli civilians into homes in the
area adjacent to Jericho, situational assessments and field patrols were
conducted to examine the incident. In the coming week, the examination of the
settlers' claims regarding the purchase of the lands will continue." The
official also said "the action was carried out without prior coordination or
approval from the IDF." They added, "The mission of the soldiers stationed at
the military outpost in the area is to safeguard the security of all residents
in the area and to prevent terror and additional confrontations."

Yet following the Israeli settlers' takeover of the homes, the Jericho
neighborhood is increasingly off limits to Palestinians or perceived
supporters. The morning after the attacks, settlers in an ATV recklessly
chased Palestinian journalists through the streets, relentlessly pursuing them
until they managed to escape the area.

Mahmoud Faridat, a resident of Al-Duyuk Al-Tahta, owns two farms directly
adjacent to the newly occupied properties. The following morning, Faridat went
to herd his sheep inside one of the farms with his brother, Jamal, and his
nephew. They were stopped by settlers, who beat Jamal and the nephew and
sprayed them with tear gas, Faridat said. Settlers had also erected another
makeshift barrier, arranging chairs and wooden planks across the road to block
access to Faridat's farmland.

"[A settler] told us not to go through it, but our water ponds and farm are
all in front of the house," Faridat told Drop Site immediately after failing
to reach his land.

"From the moment they [the settlers] came, they have attacked us." Even the
main roads in the neighborhood have become dangerous.

"The street we're standing on now is still accessible, even though the army
stops us to ask questions," Faridat said. "But tomorrow, Allah knows, they may
not let us pass at all."
